messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 49

The knife pressed cold against his ribs before his mind could process the threat. He stood frozen in the narrow lane behind the spice merchant’s shop, his leather satchel heavy with charcoal sketches, his wife’s keys dangling from his pocket. A voice cut through the humid evening air. Before he could speak, hands gripped his shoulders, pinning him against the brick wall. He watched his phone slide across the wet pavement, his keys scattering into the gutter. The man took his wallet, muttered a sharp warning, and vanished into the dark. He didn’t move until the footsteps faded. When he finally walked home, his legs felt like they belonged to someone else, his breath shallow, his mind replaying the metallic glint of the blade on repeat. The first week, he painted nothing. He sat on his studio stool, the unfinished canvases gathering dust, listening to the street every time a car door slammed or a truck backfired. He told his wife he was just exhausted, but he couldn’t explain why he checked the deadbolt five times before bed. Why he left a floor lamp burning until dawn. Why the smell of cardamom in the air now made his stomach turn. He stopped taking the alley shortcuts. He avoided the markets where strangers moved too quickly. When his wife touched his arm in the kitchen, he flinched so hard a ceramic bowl clattered to the floor. He kissed her forehead later, murmuring apologies, but the silence between them had grown heavy, textured with everything he couldn’t voice. As the weeks passed, the studio became a place of controlled breathing and scheduled daylight. He worked only while the sun was high, mixing pigments with deliberate, measured strokes, trying to anchor himself in the rhythm of bristle against primed cotton. Yet even here, his mind fractured. A dropped palette knife sent him into a sudden stillness, his pupils blowing wide, his breathing shallow. He told himself it was only metal hitting tile, but his body remembered the weight, the helplessness, the sudden narrowing of his world. He pulled the blackout curtains as the afternoon waned, not for privacy, but because he could not bear the long shadows creeping across his floor. At gallery openings, he painted portraits of acquaintances, but lately, every face seemed to look past him, searching for something he had lost. He laughed, but his laughter sounded thin, carefully placed. He noted exits. He positioned his chair facing the door. When his wife asked if they should go out for dinner, he shook his head, saying he had more to finish, though his brushes were rinsed clean, his palette scraped dry. Now, at twenty-nine, he stands at his easel, the sharp scent of linseed oil and turpentine filling the room. He has learned to recognize the early tremors in his hands before they reach his wrists. He has learned to count his breaths when the street below grows too loud. He has learned that his wife’s quiet presence in the other room is a tether he still reaches for, even when he doesn’t know how. Outside, a neighbor’s car engine sputters and dies. He doesn’t jump this time, but his jaw tightens, his fingers still on the handle of his mahlstick. He watches the street until the quiet settles, then turns back to the canvas. The paint is still wet. He dips his brush again, not because he knows what emerges, but because he has to keep his hand moving.
